title: A Wire Across the Ocean
summary: Telegraph wires could cross land, but the ocean was a huge, dark, salty problem. Brave businessmen, scientists and sailors tried again and again to lay a cable on the sea floor between Europe and America. After broken cables, a giant ship and one short-lived success, the Atlantic was finally crossed in 1866.

sections.heading: Why the Sea Is a Terrible Place for a Wire
paragraphs: Imagine trying to lay a garden hose from Ireland to Canada, along the bottom of an ocean that is in places more than 4 kilometres (about 2.5 miles) deep, without ever seeing where it lands. Then imagine that the hose has to carry tiny electric signals the whole way without leaking a drop. That was roughly the challenge facing the people who wanted to wire the world together in the 1850s.

On land, telegraph wire could be bare metal hung on poles, because dry air does not carry electricity well. Seawater is different. Salt water conducts electricity, so a bare copper wire dropped into the sea would simply leak its current into the water, like a pipe full of holes. To work underwater, a wire needs a coating, called insulation, that keeps the electricity inside. That coating must stay waterproof under enormous pressure, never crack in the cold, and last for years without rotting.

There were other problems too. A cable has to be strong enough not to snap while it is lowered from a rolling ship, yet flexible enough to coil up in the ship's hold. It has to survive anchors, rocks, currents and storms. And nobody in the 1850s really understood what would happen to an electric signal after it had travelled thousands of kilometres through a wire wrapped in insulation and surrounded by seawater. As we will see, the answer surprised almost everyone.

sections.heading: Gutta-Percha: The Sap That Wired the World
paragraphs: The solution to the insulation problem came from the rainforests of Southeast Asia. Trees of the genus Palaquium, especially Palaquium gutta, which grow in places such as the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo, ooze a milky sap when their bark is cut. When the sap dries, it becomes a tough, rubbery material. Its name, gutta-percha, comes from Malay words for the sap of the tree.

Local people had used it for a long time to make handles and other objects. In 1843 a Scottish surgeon named William Montgomerie, who worked in Singapore, brought it to the attention of scientists in Britain and was awarded a gold medal by the Royal Society of Arts. Gutta-percha had a wonderful property: dip it in hot water and it becomes soft enough to mould like clay, but let it cool and it hardens again. That meant it could be pressed around a copper wire in a smooth, seamless coat. Even better, it did not rot in seawater, and in the cold, dark depths of the ocean it lasted for years.

Scientists, including Michael Faraday and Charles Wheatstone, quickly realised that gutta-percha was an excellent insulator, which means it blocks electricity from escaping. Wheatstone suggested using it for a cable across the English Channel as early as 1845, and engineers tested gutta-percha-coated wire under rivers and in harbours in the late 1840s.

For about ninety years, almost every undersea telegraph cable in the world was insulated with gutta-percha. The demand was so huge that collectors cut down vast numbers of trees, often felling a whole tree to collect its sap, and supplies began to run short. It was an early example of how a new technology can harm a faraway environment. Gutta-percha was also used to make golf balls, called gutties, and it is still used today by dentists to fill teeth during root canal treatment. Only around 1940 did a plastic called polyethylene replace it as the main material for insulating cables.

sections.heading: First Tries Across the English Channel
paragraphs: The first big test was the English Channel, the narrow sea between England and France, only about 40 kilometres (25 miles) wide at its narrowest point. Two brothers, John Watkins Brett and Jacob Brett, formed a company to lay a cable between Dover and the French coast near Calais. In August 1850 a small steam tug called the Goliath set out, paying out a copper wire covered only in a layer of gutta-percha, with lead weights clamped to it every so often to make it sink.

It worked, at least for a little while. A few messages crossed the Channel, but then the line went silent. The thin, unprotected cable had been damaged, probably on the rocks near the French coast. A popular story says that a French fisherman hauled up the cable in his net, cut off a piece and took it home, believing he had found a strange new seaweed with gold in its middle. It is a fun tale, but it is just that: a story that historians cannot confirm.

Whatever the cause, the lesson was clear. A cable needed armour. In September 1851, the Channel was crossed again, this time with a much heavier cable. Its copper wires were insulated with gutta-percha, wrapped in tarred hemp, and then wound with a strong outer layer of iron wires, like a steel rope. It was laid from an old hulk called the Blazer, towed by tugs. This cable worked and kept working. Within months, people could send messages between London and Paris, and traders in each city could learn the other's stock and money prices in minutes rather than days.

After that, undersea cables multiplied. By 1853 cables linked Great Britain with Ireland, Belgium and the Netherlands, and others crossed straits in Denmark and the Mediterranean. Each success made a far bigger dream seem possible: a cable across the Atlantic Ocean itself, connecting Europe and North America. That would be more than fifty times longer than the Channel cable, lying in water that in places is about 4 kilometres deep instead of a few dozen metres.

sections.heading: Cyrus Field Will Not Give Up
paragraphs: The man who made the Atlantic cable happen was not a scientist or an engineer. Cyrus West Field was born in 1819 in Stockbridge, Massachusetts. At 15 he went to New York City to work as an errand boy in a big store. Later he went into the paper business and did so well that by the age of 34 he was rich enough to partly retire, with a fortune of about 250,000 dollars and a fine house in New York's Gramercy Park.

In January 1854, a British-born engineer named Frederic Newton Gisborne came to Field with a problem. Gisborne had been trying to build a telegraph line across the island of Newfoundland, the part of North America closest to Europe, so that news from ships could be flashed to New York faster. His company had run out of money. Field listened, then looked at a globe in his study, and a much bigger idea struck him. Why stop at Newfoundland? Why not keep going, right across the ocean to Ireland?

Field knew little about electricity, so he asked the experts. He wrote to Samuel Morse, who believed an ocean cable could work. He also wrote to Lieutenant Matthew Fontaine Maury of the US Navy, who studied ocean depths and currents. Ships measuring the depth of the North Atlantic with long weighted lines had found a broad, fairly level stretch of sea floor between Ireland and Newfoundland. Maury called it the Telegraph Plateau and said it seemed almost made for a cable, being deep enough to be safe from icebergs and anchors but not covered in sharp mountains.

Field threw himself into the project with astonishing energy. He first finished the land line across Newfoundland and a cable to the mainland, which alone cost more than a million dollars. Then, in 1856, he helped found the Atlantic Telegraph Company in Britain, raising money from investors on both sides of the ocean. The British and American governments both promised to lend warships and to pay for using the cable. Over the next twelve years Field crossed the Atlantic by ship dozens of times, persuading, arguing and raising money again after each disaster.

The first disaster came quickly. In August 1857, two warships, the British HMS Agamemnon and the American USS Niagara, set out from Valentia Island on the west coast of Ireland. No single ship could carry the whole cable, so each took about half. The Niagara began paying out cable from Ireland, planning to splice it to the Agamemnon's half in the middle of the ocean. But a few days out, the cable snapped and sank into water more than 3 kilometres deep. About 300 miles (480 kilometres) of expensive cable were lost on the sea floor, and the ships had to sail home.

sections.heading: 1858: A Message from the Queen
paragraphs: In 1858 the team tried a new plan. The two ships would sail to the middle of the Atlantic together, join their two halves of cable there, and then steam away from each other, one toward Ireland and one toward Newfoundland, each paying out cable behind it. That way, if something went wrong, it would happen far from land but at least the job would be shared.

The first try in June 1858 ran into one of the worst storms the sailors had ever seen. The Agamemnon, top-heavy with more than a thousand tonnes of coiled cable, rolled so violently that crew members feared she would capsize. Coal broke loose in the hold, and some sailors were injured. When the ships finally met and began laying, the cable broke several times. Again they gave up and returned to Ireland.

Field refused to quit. In July 1858 the ships sailed once more. This time, after the mid-ocean splice, everything held. On August 4, 1858, the Niagara reached Trinity Bay in Newfoundland, and the next day the Agamemnon reached Valentia Island in Ireland. For the first time in history, a single wire linked Europe and North America.

There was a lot of testing and adjusting before the cable was officially opened. On August 16, 1858, Queen Victoria sent a greeting to President James Buchanan. Her message was 98 words long, yet sending it took about 16 hours. That works out to around one word every ten minutes. The signals were so weak and blurred that operators had to repeat letters over and over before they could be sure. Buchanan replied, calling the cable a triumph that would help keep peace between nations.

Still, people went wild with joy. In New York there were parades, church bells and a huge fireworks display, so enthusiastic that the roof of City Hall caught fire. The jewellery company Tiffany bought leftover cable, cut it into short pieces and sold them as souvenirs. Newspapers called it the greatest achievement of the age.

Then the signals grew weaker and weaker. Less than three weeks after the Queen's message, in early September 1858, the cable fell silent for good. Some people even suspected the whole thing had been a hoax. It had not been: hundreds of messages had crossed, including one cancelling the departure of two British army regiments from Canada, which saved a great deal of money. But the first Atlantic cable had failed, and investors had lost a fortune. What had gone wrong?

sections.heading: Professor Thomson and the Smeared Signals
paragraphs: Part of the answer lay in a quarrel between two very different experts. One was Wildman Whitehouse, a doctor turned electrician who was the company's chief electrician. The other was William Thomson, a brilliant young physicist who had been born in Belfast in 1824 and became a professor at the University of Glasgow when he was only 22. Thomson would later be made Lord Kelvin, and the Kelvin temperature scale used by scientists today is named after him.

Scientists had already noticed something strange about long underwater cables. When you send a sharp, clean pulse of electricity into one end, it does not come out of the other end sharp and clean. It comes out late, weak and smeared, like a crisp drumbeat turned into a long, soft rumble. Michael Faraday had worked out why. A cable is a copper wire, wrapped in insulation, lying in salty water that also conducts electricity. That arrangement acts a bit like a long, thin storage tank for electric charge. Each pulse has to fill up the tank along the whole length of the cable before much current reaches the far end, and then it takes time to drain away again.

A good way to picture it is a very long, stretchy garden hose. Turn the tap on for one second and you do not get a neat one-second squirt at the far end. Instead, the hose swells, then water dribbles out slowly for a while. If you turn the tap on and off quickly, the separate squirts blur together into one long trickle. On a telegraph cable, that blurring meant dots and dashes ran into each other, so operators had to send very slowly, leaving long gaps.

In 1854 and 1855, Thomson worked out the mathematics of this effect. He showed that the delay grows with the square of the cable's length. Double the length and the signals become about four times slower. For a cable thousands of kilometres long, this was a huge problem. But Thomson's maths also showed how to fight it: use a thicker core of very pure copper, which carries current more easily, and a thicker layer of insulation. And instead of blasting the cable with powerful currents, use gentle currents and a super-sensitive detector at the far end.

Whitehouse disagreed. He believed bigger voltages were the answer, and he used huge induction coils that pushed up to about 2,000 volts into the 1858 cable. Many experts think these powerful jolts helped damage the cable's gutta-percha insulation, which already had weak spots from being stored in the sun and handled roughly. Whitehouse was dismissed. Afterwards, a special committee spent about two years studying what had happened and how to build a better cable, and many of Thomson's ideas were adopted.

sections.heading: A Mirror on a Silk Thread
paragraphs: Thomson's most famous gadget for the cable was the mirror galvanometer, which he patented in 1858. A galvanometer is a device that detects electric current. Ordinary ones used a needle that swung when current flowed, but on a long ocean cable the current arriving at the far end was so feeble that a normal needle would hardly twitch.

Thomson's clever solution was to make the moving part almost weightless. He glued tiny magnets to the back of a small, light, round mirror and hung it on a single fine thread inside a coil of wire. When even a very weak current flowed through the coil, the magnets twisted slightly and the mirror tilted. A lamp shone a beam of light onto the mirror, which reflected it onto a scale on the wall, several feet away. Because the light beam acted like a very long, weightless pointer, a tiny tilt of the mirror made the spot of light jump a large distance along the scale.

Operators sat in a darkened room watching the bright spot dance left and right. A swing one way meant a dot, a swing the other way meant a dash. With this delicate instrument, a cable could be worked with gentle currents that did not harm its insulation. Later, in 1867, Thomson invented the siphon recorder, which used a tiny ink tube to draw the signals as a wavy line on moving paper tape, so the message could be checked afterwards.

Thomson's ideas also shaped the new cable itself. The cable planned for the next attempt had a much heavier copper core and much thicker gutta-percha insulation than the 1858 one. It was protected by iron wires each wrapped in tarred hemp, which made it strong but also much heavier. In fact, it was so heavy and bulky that no ordinary ship could carry all of it. Luckily, there was one ship in the world big enough.

sections.heading: The Great Eastern Saves the Day
paragraphs: The SS Great Eastern was the giant of its age. Designed by the famous engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel and launched on the River Thames in London in 1858, it was about 211 metres (692 feet) long, longer than two football fields, and was built to carry about 4,000 passengers all the way to Australia without stopping for coal. It had both huge paddle wheels and a propeller. But as a passenger ship it was a disappointment. It was expensive to run, and it never filled up. For years it seemed like a giant white elephant.

For cable laying, though, it was perfect. Its enormous holds could carry the entire Atlantic cable, thousands of kilometres of it, in giant water-filled tanks that kept the gutta-percha cool. That meant no risky splice in mid-ocean. Its huge size also made it steadier in rough seas than smaller ships, and it carried enough coal for the whole trip.

In July 1865 the Great Eastern set out from Ireland, paying out the new cable over its stern. Field and Thomson were both on board. Engineers on deck constantly tested the cable as it went down, and several times they had to haul faulty sections back up to repair them. Then, on August 2, 1865, after more than 1,000 nautical miles (about 2,000 kilometres) had been laid, the cable snapped and slid into water more than 3 kilometres deep. The crew lowered grappling hooks on long ropes and actually caught the cable several times, but each time the rope broke before the cable reached the surface. Once again, the ship returned home defeated.

Field and his partners raised new money and formed a new company. On July 13, 1866, the Great Eastern left Valentia Island again with a fresh, improved cable. This time the voyage went smoothly. On July 27, 1866, the giant ship arrived at the little fishing village of Heart's Content in Newfoundland, and the cable was brought ashore. Europe and North America were connected again, and this time the connection lasted.

Then the Great Eastern did something even more amazing. It sailed back out to where the 1865 cable had been lost. Over many days, the crew dragged grappling hooks along the ocean floor, more than 3 kilometres below. It was like trying to pick up a piece of string from the bottom of a deep lake while standing on a moving boat in the dark. At the start of September they finally lifted the old cable to the surface, tested it, and found the signal from Ireland still came through. They spliced on new cable and landed it at Heart's Content on September 7, 1866. Now there were two working Atlantic cables. The ship's first officer, Robert Halpin, who helped find the lost cable, later became her captain and laid more cables around the world.

sections.heading: News in Minutes Instead of Days
paragraphs: The 1866 cable changed the speed of the world. The 1858 cable had managed only about one-tenth of a word per minute. The new cable could carry around eight words per minute, and later improvements made it faster still. A piece of news that had needed about ten days to cross the Atlantic by steamship could now cross in minutes.

At first, sending a cable message, often called a cablegram, was extremely expensive. In the early days a message of twenty words reportedly cost about 20 British pounds, more than many workers earned in months. So most users were governments, newspapers, banks and big merchants. Traders in London and New York could now know each other's prices almost the same day, and newspapers could print European news while it was still fresh. Governments could discuss problems quickly instead of waiting weeks for letters, which sometimes helped calm disagreements before they grew.

The heroes were rewarded. William Thomson was knighted in 1866, becoming Sir William, partly for his cable work. In 1867 the United States Congress gave Cyrus Field a gold medal. Field later lost much of his fortune through bad investments, but his headstone in Stockbridge says the world owes the Atlantic telegraph to his courage, energy and perseverance.

Over the next few decades, more and more cables were laid. Cables soon reached India, Australia, South America and Asia, and by the end of the century a web of undersea wires linked most of the world's major countries. A message could travel from London to Bombay or from New York to Cape Town in hours. Historians sometimes call this network the Victorian internet, because for the first time the whole planet could share news almost at once.

Yet every one of these cables still did the same simple thing as Morse's first line: it carried clicks. Short pulses and long pulses, dots and dashes, letter by letter. Nobody could talk through them. And that raised a new and even more daring question. If electricity could carry clicks under a whole ocean, could it be made to carry something much more complicated and beautiful: the sound of a human voice?

deepDive: The physics behind the 1858 failure and the 1866 success is one of the founding stories of electrical engineering. A submarine cable is a conductor separated from the conducting seawater by a thin layer of insulation, so it behaves as a long distributed capacitor in series with the resistance of the copper core. Faraday and Latimer Clark observed the resulting signal retardation in the early 1850s, and in 1854–55 William Thomson modelled it with the same diffusion equation used for heat flow. His result, often called the 'law of squares' or 'KR law', says the time a pulse takes to build up at the far end is proportional to the cable's total resistance multiplied by its total capacitance, and since both grow with length, the delay scales with the square of the length. Whitehouse, a medical man with practical experience but little theory, doubted the law, argued that results from short test lengths would scale up, and favoured high-voltage induction coils. The 1858 cable had a thin core of uneven-quality copper and insulation that had been damaged during storage and laying; most historians conclude that its faults were made worse by Whitehouse's high voltages, though the cable was probably doomed anyway. After the failure, a joint committee of the British Board of Trade and the Atlantic Telegraph Company (1859–1861) produced a landmark report on cable design, testing and materials, helping turn telegraph engineering into a science based on measurement. Standard units of resistance and other electrical quantities, eventually including the ohm, grew partly out of this need to specify cable properties precisely. The 1866 cable reflected Thomson's prescriptions: a core of high-conductivity copper about three times heavier per mile than in 1858, thicker gutta-percha, and sensitive low-voltage detection. Later, Oliver Heaviside extended Thomson's analysis by including inductance, work that would matter greatly for telephone lines. Economically, cable rates fell over time from the very high 1866 tariff, and by 1900 British companies owned most of the world's cable network, a fact historians link to British commercial and imperial power.
funFact: When the 1858 Atlantic cable was celebrated in New York, the fireworks display was so enthusiastic that it set the roof of City Hall on fire.
